sweep_summary: One works with stress in the title for Ao Naga (aona1235, catalog: no-word-stress on Coupe 2003): Temsunungsang 2009, the EFLU Hyderabad PhD thesis on Ao prosodic phonology. Abstract, contents and chapters 1, 2 and 5 were already held by the project from the 2026-09-16 check; I extracted the chapter 1-2 text and read the stress passages. Chapter 5 (pp. 118, 130, 147) states outright that Ao lacks a stress system (no evidence from intensity, duration or pitch; tone not attracted to any position) and builds foot structure from tone and minimality instead; chapter 2 adds that vowel reduction is consonant-conditioned, not stress-conditioned. This CONFIRMS the catalog's classification as an independent native-speaker source; it does not supersede Coupe 2003, whose acoustic measurements remain the deciding record. Attempts to download the remaining chapters (3, 4, 6, bibliography) failed: Shodhganga timed out on all hosts today (low priority, chapter 5 is the stress chapter). Two other held Ao sources re-checked: Temsunungsang & Changkija 2025 (Changki-Ao phonology) has no stress statement; Walling 2017 ch. 3 mentions stress only in general remarks about tone languages. for the session was exhausted (2000/2000), so no new title hunting beyond the Crossref record already held (Temsunungsang 2008 'Tonality and the analysis of sub-minimal words in Ao', doi 10.1017/upo9788175968431.005, not a stress title). written at

new_statements.quote: A noteworthy characteristic of Mongsen words is their lack of phonemic stress. All syllables of polysyllabic words tend to be equally weighted with respect to the possible perceptual correlates of stress, such as duration, intensity and loudness. Pitch, a fourth possible perceptual correlate of stress commonly utilized by the world's languages, is monopolized by the lexical tone and intonation systems of Mongsen, thus cannot be exploited for the purpose of giving prominence to a particular syllable in a polysyllabic word.

tone_statements.quote: Chungli shows a three way tonal contrast and bear a tone on every syllable, either lexically or by default. The three contrastive tones attested are High, Mid and Low. ... While all the three tones can be realised on smooth syllables, only the High and Low tones are attested in checked syllables. ... A single syllable can also have a maximum of two tones. However, this is treated as the concatenation of two level tones rather than as a contour tone since they do not show any contrast. The tones are realised on the vowels or the coda if it is a sonorant.
tone_statements.summary: Chungli Ao: three level tones H, M, L on every syllable; only H and L in checked syllables; two-tone syllables analysed as level sequences, not contours. Minimal triplet áʧə́m/āʧə̄m/áʧə̀m given.

tone_statements.citation: Bruhn, Daniel. 2009. The tonal classification of Chungli Ao verbs. UC Berkeley Phonology Lab Annual Report 5. Berkeley: University of California. doi 10.5070/P722C6C7D9.
tone_statements.quote: Chungli Ao exhibits a register tone system. The tone-bearing unit is the syllable, and three tone levels exist: high (H), mid (M), and low (L). The H tone has a limited distribution, and usually appears before a L tone in a disyllabic H.L pattern or monosyllabic HL contour. The only underlying contour tones on monosyllables are HL and LM, though HM contours can surface when HL is followed by a syllable bearing M or H. Across word classes, the most common tone patterns for disyllables are M.M and H.L, with L.L and L.M less common. M.L and H.H patterns are very rare and/or marginal.
tone_statements.locator: p. 66, sec. 2.3 Tones; footnote numbers 2, 3 elided
tone_statements.summary: Three level tones H M L on the syllable; HL, LM contours on monosyllables as level sequences; upstep rule M->H before L (Table 5); floating M posited after Class 2 verb stems; suffixes bear tones.

tone_statements.citation: Coupe, Alexander R. 1998. The acoustic and perceptual features of tone in the Tibeto-Burman language Ao Naga. In R. Mannell & J. Robert-Ribes (eds), Proceedings of the 5th International Conference on Spoken Language Processing (ICSLP 1998), Sydney, paper 0688. ISCA. doi 10.21437/ICSLP.1998-102.
tone_statements.quote: The auditory analysis identifies three tonemes occurring on all six vowels and on all syllable types. The high toneme ranges from integers 4 to 5; the mid toneme has its focus at 3, but may be as low as 2 or as high as 4; and the low toneme ranges from 1 to 2. Levels are not absolute and may therefore overlap; in the absence of phonological cues such as a distinctive pitch contours or differences in duration, what is held to be phonemically significant is the pitch level relative to that of preceding and/or following syllables.
tone_statements.summary: Three level tonemes, F0 only 10-20 Hz apart but perceptually reliable; a falling [53] on 'and'/conjunctive suffixes set aside as clause-marking. (H) and ~ (L).

sources.note: First-hand phonological study of Chungli and Mongsen Ao by a native-speaker linguist. States repeatedly that Ao has no stress system: no evidence for stress from intensity, duration or pitch, and tones show no attraction to any word position. Foot structure is argued for on other grounds (disyllabic minimality, vowel augmentation, schwa deletion, binary tone spreading); the author proposes a violable right-aligned trochaic foot and a tonal foot built from de Lacy's tonal prominence hierarchy (H most prominent), explicitly 'without reference to traditional stress related' factors. sources.quote: Chungli shows a three way tonal contrast and bear a tone on every syllable, either lexically or by default. The three contrastive tones attested are High, Mid and Low. ... While all the three tones can be realised on smooth syllables, only the High and Low tones are attested in checked syllables. ... A single syllable can also have a maximum of two tones. However, this is treated as the concatenation of two level tones rather than as a contour tone since they do not show any contrast. The tones are realised on the vowels or the coda if it is a sonorant.

sources.quote: Chungli Ao exhibits a register tone system. The tone-bearing unit is the syllable, and three tone levels exist: high (H), mid (M), and low (L). The H tone has a limited distribution, and usually appears before a L tone in a disyllabic H.L pattern or monosyllabic HL contour. The only underlying contour tones on monosyllables are HL and LM, though HM contours can surface when HL is followed by a syllable bearing M or H. Across word classes, the most common tone patterns for disyllables are M.M and H.L, with L.L and L.M less common. M.L and H.H patterns are very rare and/or marginal.

sources.quote: The auditory analysis identifies three tonemes occurring on all six vowels and on all syllable types. The high toneme ranges from integers 4 to 5; the mid toneme has its focus at 3, but may be as low as 2 or as high as 4; and the low toneme ranges from 1 to 2. Levels are not absolute and may therefore overlap; in the absence of phonological cues such as a distinctive pitch contours or differences in duration, what is held to be phonemically significant is the pitch level relative to that of preceding and/or following syllables.
sources.note: Three level tonemes, F0 only 10-20 Hz apart but perceptually reliable; a falling [53] on 'and'/conjunctive suffixes set aside as clause-marking. (H) and ~ (L).
